title: Python GC + epoll interaction causing bursty latency spikes (investigation notes)
content:
Summary:

Observed periodic tail-latency spikes (~p99-p999) on the hosted API when small bursts of requests arrive (bursts = 50-200 reqs/sec for ~200-800ms). Median and p95 are stable; p99/p999 move dramatically (p99 from ~45ms to 280-420ms depending on load). This note collates profiling evidence pointing to an interaction between Python GC, epoll wait wakeups, and our tokenization/request-parse hot paths.

Context / hypothesis:
- We serve many short requests that are parse/tokenize + model call. Tokenizer is a C-extension but we allocate short-lived Python objects around it for metadata and parsing.
- The server uses a mix of threads (acceptor + io threads) and a ThreadPoolExecutor for blocking preproc (tokenization + request decode).
- We saw that GC collections (non-controversial) coincide with short periods where many worker threads are paused and then wake up simultaneously causing kernel scheduling + epoll wake storms and eventual queueing at the runtime boundary.
- Hypothesis: GC (and in particular generation-2 collections) are triggering synchronous pauses in many threads; combined with epoll wake/wakeup costs and our per-request allocations causes bursts in syscalls and scheduler overhead leading to observed tail spikes.

Evidence collected:
1) Timeline correlation
- From logs and metrics: every p99 spike maps to a ~5-30ms duration where a subset of worker threads show 100% time in 'syscall' and 'stop-the-world' like markers.
- Heap / GC traces (pyperf + tracemalloc sampling): we see generation promotions preceding spikes; memory allocations ramp up for ~100ms before GC.

2) Profiling snapshots (linux perf + py-spy)
- During normal steady-state: tokenization C-extension shows ~30% of CPU in C token code, Python overhead (object alloc/free) ~12%.
- During burst spike: profile shows long stack traces in epoll_wait -> accept4 -> read (syscall), and Python threads stuck in GC safepoint routines.
- py-spy flamegraph (sampled) shows a block where most Python threads' stacks are in 'collect_garbage' and 'PyObject_Malloc' frames.

3) Tracer output (application-level)
- Request enter times are clustered (burst), many requests finish preproc quickly but then tasks are scheduled onto executor and appear to be delayed by ~200ms before model_dispatch.
- Thread state dumps show many threads in 'WAITING' for the GIL or blocked in GC.

Microbench experiments run locally:
- Synthetic harness: spawn 100 short requests/sec that do: json.loads(200B) + tokenizer.tokenize(12 tokens) + minor metadata allocations.
- Baseline (GC enabled default): p99 = 310ms, p95 = 48ms.
- With gc.disable() during bulk preproc path: p99 = 62ms, p95 = 46ms.
- With allocated object reuse pool (reuse bytearrays) + gc tuning (thresholds increased): p99 = 78ms.
- Using process-based worker pool (multiprocessing) instead of threads: p99 = 72ms but 2x memory.

System-level traces:
- strace on a worker during spike shows many epoll_wait/epoll_pwait with small timeouts and wakeups for many fds; then a sudden cluster of read returns and Python syscalls (madvise, mallinfo) around GC.
- /proc/schedstat shows scheduling latency spikes aligned with GC times.

Root causes (proposed):
- Frequent short-lived allocations cause generation promotion and more frequent gen2 collections under burst load.
- The CPython GC pauses are global for the interpreter; in multi-threaded programs this leads to many threads paused concurrently (not just GIL, but GC safepoint overhead).
- Epoll and kernel wakeups amplify the effect: when many sockets become readable at once, threads wake and try to allocate/parse, stepping on GC scheduling and causing contention.
- Our threadpool size and task granularity (many tiny tasks) make us more sensitive to GC pauses.

Mitigations attempted and results:
- gc.disable() around preprocessing (unsafe globally): massively improved tail but risk of memory growth. Feasible as a targeted optimization if we force a manual collect at controlled times (see next).
- bump gc thresholds (gc.set_threshold(7000, 10, 10)): reduced frequency of GCs, p99 improved ~40%, but memory footprint rose ~15%.
- object pooling for bytes/bytearray used in request parsing: p99 improved ~20% and reduced allocations captured by tracemalloc.
- switch to multiprocessing workers (process pool) for tokenization: removes GC interactions with main process but increases memory and increases cold-start cost for worker processes; tail improved but operational cost up.
- move tokenization to a native C threadpool (no Python allocations): best latency improvements but increased complexity (needs robust FFI).

Detailed experiment notes (commands, reproducible steps):
- Harness: ./tools/sim_burst --rate=100 --burst-width=300ms --payload=sample-json.json --concurrency=400 --duration=120s --endpoint=http://localhost:8000/v1/pred
- Baseline run: ./run_bench.sh baseline -> collect p99.
- Disable GC test: export PREPROC_NO_GC=1 (branch sets gc.disable() around preproc) -> run harness.
- Pooling test: run branch reuse-buffers (PR discussed).
- Multiprocess test: run branch multiprocessing-workers.

Observations on tokenization vs parsing costs:
- Tokenizer C-ext is cheap (2-6ms per call), but JSON parsing/metadata assembly in Python is ~4-10ms and generates most allocations.
- Combining JSON parse + tokenizer in a pooled native buffer reduces allocations significantly.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are we seeing any memory fragmentation in allocator (jemalloc/malloc) that triggers more frequent GC? Need allocation profiler with allocation sizes.
- How much of the observed scheduler delay is from epoll wake bursts vs actual GC safepoint mechanics? Can we reproduce with synthetic epoll-only burst (no allocations)?
- Interaction with network stack: do we get packet coalescing or NIC interrupts that cluster arrivals? NIC config could be amplifying bursts.

Proposed short-term mitigations (low risk):
1) Increase GC thresholds modestly in hot-path workers (configurable env var) to reduce gen2 frequency. Add a memory watchdog that triggers collection when RSS crosses threshold. (RW-2123)
2) Implement targeted gc.disable() during the preproc critical section and call gc.collect() after N requests or every X ms as a cooperative strategy. Wrap carefully and monitor RSS.
3) Object reuse for request parsing: preallocate bytearray buffers per worker and reuse to avoid allocations. This is low-risk and already rolled up in PR #487.
4) Tune threadpool sizing and task batching: prefer batching small tokenization tasks into a single task to reduce scheduling overhead.

Proposed medium-term mitigations (higher effort):
1) Move JSON parsing and tokenization into a native module (C/C++) that returns token IDs in a preallocated buffer. Avoid Python-level allocations for hot path.
2) Offer an optional dedicated preproc process pool (multiprocess) for tenants with high short-request patterns. Trade memory for tail latency.
3) Investigate switching to subinterpreters (PEP 554 style) or specialized runtimes (PyPy) for better GC behavior; evaluate compatibility costs.

Monitoring + Metrics we should add:
- Expose GC pause metrics (time spent in GC), allocation rate, promoted object counts at per-worker granularity.
- Metric: fraction of requests that experience > X ms delay between preproc_complete and model_dispatch.
- Heatmap of request arrival clustering (inter-arrival CDF) per route.
- Track RSS vs p99 to see trade-offs when we tune GC thresholds.

Next actions / TODOs:
- [Priya] Draft a small targeted change to disable GC around preproc with explicit gc.collect() every 500ms; push canary on staging. (ETA: 2025-10-07)
- [Marcus] Run allocator-level sampling to see big-allocation contributors and check jemalloc stats. (ETA: 2025-09-30)
- [Ava] Instrument epoll wake counts and create a trace that isolates kernel wake/wakeup overhead. (ETA: 2025-10-05)
- [Samir] Measure memory increase for raising GC thresholds to find safe ceiling per-instance. (ETA: 2025-10-02)

Risk notes:
- Disabling GC without a robust collection policy can OOM in long-running instances; need memory watchdogs.
- Multiprocessing increases memory per replica and complicates cold-starts and tracing.
- Native C modules require thorough fuzz testing for correctness and resilience against malformed inputs.

Appendix: quick reproducible summary
- Repro script: tools/sim_burst + branch preproc-gc-toggle. Run baseline and gc-disabled runs and compare profiles.
- Useful commands:
  - py-spy record -o flame.svg --pid <worker-pid> --duration 30s
  - python -m tracemalloc to capture allocation snapshots around bursts
  - sudo perf record -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30 ; sudo perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf-flame.svg

Notes to reviewer:
- This doc is a working investigation; the aim is to pick 1 low-risk mitigation (pooled buffers + gc tuning) to canary next week, and run the more invasive options (native preproc or process pool) as part of the Q4 perf roadmap.
- Feedback welcome on empiric thresholds for memory watchdog and preferred config knobs exposed to customers (per-instance env vars vs global runtime defaults).

References and related tickets:
